job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Maya Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat in Sunvale with my grandmother Dona Lucia and my aunt Teresa. Grandma wakes me at seven with the radio on, we have breakfast together, and then I'm at the dining table with my laptop until noon, applying for jobs in manufacturing and production. In the afternoons I take Grandma to the market or the clinic, and twice a week I help my aunt with her accounts, since she runs a small catering business. We go to Mass on Sunday, and I always see someone who asks about my job hunt.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and how has the search been?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied industrial and manufacturing engineering and finished in June with a good result. My final project was a layout redesign for a small packaging line, and I did a ten-week internship at a food-packaging plant called Valley Foods, working on line efficiency. They were happy with me, but hiring is frozen. I've sent about sixty-five applications and had three interviews. I'm carrying heavy student debt, I've got around a week and a half of costs saved, and the family helps with food and a bed, but no cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's reassuring, and I'd say I told you so to my cousin who was convinced he'd be out of work. At Mass or at the market, I'd say that most things stay as they are and we keep working. Then I'd go home and keep applying, because reassurance doesn't pay a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a plateau means my situation stays what it is. There are few plants nearby, and Valley Foods says it won't hire until spring at the earliest. My loan payments start soon, and my savings are thin. I'm not scared of change, but I am worried about the slow grind of nothing happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying to manufacturing jobs in a wider area, maybe up to an hour away, and I'd say yes to a temporary production planner post, even for a short time. I'd ask Mr Almeida, my supervisor at Valley, if he'll recommend me to others. I'd keep doing my aunt's accounts for a bit of pay, and I'd start studying for a lean manufacturing certificate, which isn't expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Patient, mostly, but with a knot in my chest that tightens when the loan letter arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you actually do at the packaging plant, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I walked the line with a stopwatch and a clipboard, timing how long each step took. Then I made a plan to move two machines closer together, which saved the operators about twenty minutes a shift. It felt good to see something I'd drawn on paper change the way people worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family say about the job hunt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're supportive, but they don't know what to say. Grandma says God will provide, and I believe her, but I also know the electricity bill doesn't read the Bible. My aunt says come and work for her full time, which is kind, but catering doesn't pay a loan either.

say: I'd say reassurance is fine, but it doesn't pay a **loan**.
At Mass and the market I'd say most things stay as they are and we keep working.
think: A plateau keeps things as they are, with few plants nearby and Valley Foods **frozen** until spring.
I'm not scared of change, but I'm worried about the slow grind.
do: Apply to manufacturing jobs up to an hour away, including a **temporary** production planner post.
Ask Mr Almeida at Valley Foods to recommend me.
Start a lean manufacturing certificate and keep doing my aunt's accounts.
feel: **Patient**, with a knot in my chest when the loan letter arrives.
Quiet worry that doesn't go away.
S0.quote: Grandma says God will provide, and I believe her, but I also know the electricity bill doesn't read the Bible.
fieldNote: Her **faith** and family are steady, but she is clear that bills need money.
She wants any production job, even a **temporary** one, to get a foot in.
The stopwatch story shows she likes seeing her work change a real **workplace**.

steps.text: Apply to manufacturing jobs up to an hour away
Take a temporary production planner post if offered
Do the books for my aunt's catering business for pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change we need to take seriously, and workers and firms should talk about it honestly. I'd tell my friends at church that machines have come and gone before, and families have always found ways through. But I'd also say companies must train people, not just replace them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. Planning, scheduling, checking and efficiency studies are thinking tasks, and software can do a lot of them. At Valley, a planner told me an AI tool would give her the weekly schedule in minutes, which used to take half a day. That's the kind of job I want. But the machines on the floor still need people to move, fix and set up, so the plant needs people who understand both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to become that person who understands both the line and the software. I'd learn how the scheduling tools work and I'd do a short course on automation and robotics maintenance. I'd also apply to maintenance and quality roles, where people are still on the floor. I'd try an AI tool for my aunt's accounts to see what it saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense, but I'm not frightened yet. It feels like when the plant changes shifts, and you have to rearrange your whole life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of line efficiency work would software take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The scheduling, the layout calculations and the reports. At the packaging plant where I interned, I made one efficiency report in a week and the software company's demo made one in ten minutes. What it doesn't do is notice that a worker is limping or that a machine sounds odd. That's a person walking the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use more AI at home or at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more, yes. I use it now and then for summaries, and the results are okay if I check them. For my aunt's accounts I'd try it on receipts and invoices. I won't hand it anything I can't check, because accounts are someone's living.

say: I'd tell friends machines have come before and families found ways through, but firms must **train** people.
Workers and firms should talk about it honestly.
think: Scheduling and efficiency studies are thinking tasks, and one planner told me an AI tool does a half-day job in **minutes**.
The plant still needs people who understand the line and the software.
do: Become the person who understands both the line and the **software**.
Take a short course in automation and robotics maintenance.
Apply for maintenance and quality roles, and try AI on my aunt's accounts.
feel: A bit **tense**, but not frightened yet.
Like when a shift changes and you rearrange your whole life.
S1.quote: At the packaging plant where I interned, I made one efficiency report in a week and the software company's demo made one in ten minutes.
fieldNote: She has a **concrete** example from the plant that shapes her view.
Her plan is to be the **bridge** between floor and software.
She will try AI on her aunt's books but refuses to hand it what she cannot **check**.

steps.text: Take a short course in automation and robotics maintenance
Apply for plant maintenance and quality jobs
Try an AI tool on my aunt's invoices and receipts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after each other, and I'd say it to the parish and to the council. Governments must slow it down or provide for people, and companies need to carry some of the cost. I'd say all this in a calm voice, because panic is the worst response.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm very afraid. Two years is too soon. I'd just be starting out, and the planning and scheduling work I trained for would go first, then the line work three years later. I'd be competing with machines that don't need rest, and I'd still owe the loan. I don't see an obvious place for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job that has a wage, whether it's on the line or in the stores, and keep living in the flat. I'd stop my certificates and save everything. I'd ask the parish about support. I'd learn a hands-on skill like machine repair, since the robots take a few years longer. And I'd help my aunt turn the catering into something that could pay us both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Sad, too. I think of Grandma, who's eighty, and I feel I've let her down because I haven't started paying my own way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandmother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with her and take her hand and tell her what's happening in plain words. She'd listen, and then she'd say, we've been through the war and the hunger, we'll get through this. I'd cry afterwards in the kitchen. She makes me feel small and strong at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Valley Foods and plants like it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd try to hang on as long as possible, and then they'd bring in machines to run the planning and the line. The owners will do fine. The question is what happens to the two hundred people who work at the packaging plant where I interned. Half of them are in my parish.

say: I'd say we need to look after each other, and **governments** must slow it down or provide for people.
I'd say it calmly, because panic is the worst response.
think: Two years is too soon: my planning skills go first, and I'd still owe the **loan**.
I don't see an obvious place for me.
do: Take any job with a **wage**, on the line or in the stores, and keep living in the flat.
Stop the certificates, save everything and ask the parish about support.
Learn machine repair and help my aunt grow the catering business.
feel: **Heavy** and sad, as if I've let down my grandmother.
Small and strong at the same time.
S2.quote: The question is what happens to the two hundred people who work at the packaging plant where I interned. Half of them are in my parish.
fieldNote: Her fear is **communal**: the parish and the plant workers matter as much as her own job.
She sees the **three-year** gap for hands-on work and plans machine repair for it.
Guilt toward her eighty-year-old grandmother is a **driver**.

steps.text: Take any wage-paying job on the line or in the stores
Stop all spending on certificates and save every pound
Learn machine repair at a local college
Ask the parish about support for the family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare, but we have to start. I'd tell my cousins and friends not to wait. I'd say it at the parish meeting, too, that we could set up a small group to help people retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's better than two, but it's still tight. I think I could get a first job, maybe two years of experience, and then be in a good place to move into maintenance or automation. I'd have the loan partly paid. But I'd still be young, and the planning jobs I want are the ones software gets first. So I'm hopeful but I'm not relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a production or maintenance job, anything on a floor. I'd put a third of my pay into the loan, and I'd study automation and maintenance in the evenings. After a year or so I'd ask the firm to put me on the robot projects. I'd also help my aunt grow the catering side, just a little, so there's a family fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than two years. Not good, but better. There's something to work towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would five years change what you'd do in the first twelve months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd prefer to, because of Grandma and the parish. But if the right job were an hour away I'd rent a room during the week and come home on weekends. I wouldn't move to another city, I don't think. That's a line I'd draw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to stay in Sunvale?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Having five years, I'd be more careful about the order. First the job, then the loan, then the training. With two years I'd panic and do all of it badly. I'm steady, and I do better when there's a sequence.

say: I'd say five years is enough to prepare but we have to **start**.
At the parish I'd suggest a small group to help people retrain.
think: It's better than two but still tight, and the planning jobs I want are the ones software gets **first**.
do: Take a production or **maintenance** job, then study automation in the evenings.
Put a third of my pay into the loan.
Ask my employer to put me on robot projects and help my aunt grow the catering.
feel: **Better** than two years, with something to work towards.
S3.quote: I'm steady, and I do better when there's a sequence.
fieldNote: She wants a **sequence**: job, loan, training, and she says she does better with it.
Distance is acceptable during the week, but **leaving** the city she knows is a line she draws.
The parish group shows her instinct to **organise** locally.

steps.text: Take a production or maintenance job on a factory floor
Put a third of every pay cheque into the loan
Study automation and maintenance in the evenings
Help my aunt grow the catering side a little

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long time and we have no excuse not to be ready. I'd tell people to keep their families close, keep working, and build something that lasts. I'd say the faith community can be a place to share skills and help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm much less afraid. Ten years lets me get a job, work my way up and probably have a family. By then I'd be thirty-three, married, perhaps, and in a job I've grown into. The machines will come, but I'd be someone who knows the plant and the people, and that's useful. I'd still worry about the loan, but I can handle a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work my way through production and maintenance, and aim for a supervisor role at about year five. I'd pay down the loan, save for a deposit on a small flat near Grandma's, and take a course in automation. I'd think about marrying, and having my own family. And I'd help my aunt turn the catering into a proper small business with a real kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of worry, but the normal kind, the kind you have when you're building something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you hope to build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope to have a steady job, a home, a family and a bit of land, if I could. Nothing grand. I'd want to still be near Grandma's grave and the parish in thirty years, and to have helped my aunt's business reach a second kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousins who are still at school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get a skill with their hands and a skill with their heads, and not to be ashamed of either. The people who understand both will be the ones the plant can't do without.

The faith community can share skills and help each other.
think: I'm much less afraid, and I'd be someone who knows the plant and the **people**.

Pay down the loan and save for a deposit on a small flat.
Help my aunt turn her catering into a proper small business.
feel: **Calm**, with the normal worry of building something.

fieldNote: Her hopes are modest and **local**: a flat near her grandmother, a family and the parish.
She uses the decade to plan a **career ladder** to supervisor.
Her aunt's catering business is a recurring **family** project.

steps.text: Aim for a production supervisor role by year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is short for a girl with a loan and no savings, and the planning side of my work goes first. What would help is steady and practical: first jobs with training, a pause on loan payments while work is scarce, and local support, like parish and council groups that help families. And a bit of honesty from the people in charge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not asking for a miracle. I come from people who work hard and don't complain. If somebody gave me a first job and a fair chance, I'd work like my grandmother did. I'd want people to remember that families are what hold things up when jobs go, so don't forget them in the plans.

headlineQuote: I come from people who work hard and don't complain. If somebody gave me a first job and a fair chance, I'd work like my grandmother did.
portrait: Maya is a **23-year-old** industrial engineering graduate living with her grandmother and aunt, with sixty-five applications, three interviews and no offer.
She did a packaging-line project and a ten-week plant internship, and has heavy debt with about **ten days** of costs saved.
She is traditional and faith-minded, draws strength from the parish and family, and wants work over handouts.
Steady and open to proven change, she uses AI now and then and plans **sequences**: job, loan, training.
She is anxious in most pictures, alarmed with two years, and uneasy with ten.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries her most, because the planning side of her work goes first and the debt stays.
whatWouldHelp: First jobs with **training**, paused loan payments while work is scarce, and parish and council support for families.
